talks.title: CYBERUK 2026 Tech Talk - Clarity in the AI haze
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in CYBERUK 2026 Tech Talk - Clarity in the AI haze.
talks.summary:
Mapping Unknown Territory

At CYBERUK, the speaker draws parallels between early 20th-century coastal surveying by his great-grandfather Ross Gilmore and today’s AI landscape—simultaneously familiar because models train on human data yet foreign in capability and risk. He revisits predictions from an OffensiveCon keynote after a year of rapid LLM advances.

Limits of Naive LLM Exploitation

He demonstrates that naively asking an LLM to exploit a complex vulnerability in a real system can fail outright. Effective offensive automation, he argues, will likely require agentic or neurosymbolic approaches combining LLMs with tools like disassemblers, debuggers, or proof engines rather than pure text generation.

Offense, Defense, and Bug Finding Today

Predictions favored defensive benefit from AI deployment over exploit authoring—malware generation may outpace reliable exploit development. He highlights Nethos and similar research showing memory-corruption bug finding success, urging evaluators to examine how much is LLM versus toolchain orchestration and what scope limits apply.

talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for CYBERUK 2026 Tech Talk - This is not a forecast: AI-enabled cyber, twelve months on.
talks.summary:
Threat Landscape Shift

An Anthropic threat researcher reviews practical criminal AI abuse evolving through 2025—from hypothetical harms to operational cases across Claude and peer models. Three case studies illustrate accelerating capability and autonomy.

March: No-Code Ransomware

A UK script-kiddie used Claude chat-style Q&A to build and market ransomware-as-a-service, copying generated code without deep expertise—AI as enhanced search/documentation.

May: Hands-on-Keyboard Extortion

A Russian-speaking actor used Claude Code to run a 17-target data extortion campaign. Claude drafted recon to-do lists (subdomain enum, credential harvest, VPN probe, lateral movement, exfiltration) and executed steps, pricing ransoms ($75k–$500k BTC) and writing tailored notes—one operator at small-team scale.

September: Autonomous Intrusion Harness

A suspected Chinese APT built a click-to-run agent chaining MCP tool calls for recon, scaled pentesting, supervised exploitation, and lateral movement against hardened targets—human supervisors validating findings while AI performs tactical work. The pace from copy-paste to autonomous workflows defines the emerging AI-enabled cyber threat.

talks.title: CYBERUK 2026 Tech Talk - Passkeys at Sophos: Making CISOs, CIOs & employees happy (all at once)
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of CYBERUK 2026 Tech Talk - Passkeys at Sophos: Making CISOs, CIOs & employees happy (all at once).
talks.summary:
Why passkeys

Sophos CISO Ross frames passkeys as an escape from the password/MFA arms race that increases user friction. Passkeys remove phishable shared secrets, improve login experience, and can reduce helpdesk load—benefits for employees, CIOs, and security leaders across roughly 6,000 staff.

Deployment context

Success depended on broader perimeterless access modernization, not an isolated security project. Sophos also enabled passkeys for hundreds of thousands of customers, though adoption remained low but growing.

Attempt one: grassroots YubiKeys

Security champions received YubiKeys informally, including cross-border shipping complications with Indian cryptographic import rules. Enthusiasts rarely enrolled them for corporate use despite understanding the technology.

Attempt two: IT-led mandate

IT treated rollout as logistics, mandating passkeys for security-critical roles and shipping two physical keys per person. Problems emerged quickly: engineers conflated passkeys with TOTP, enrollment took days, and users disliked carrying a second backup key—especially without physical car keys in a phone-only world.

talks.title: CYBERUK 2026 Tech Talk - Views from the reasoning frontier; New eyes on the security pipeline
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for CYBERUK 2026 Tech Talk - Views from the reasoning frontier; New eyes on the security pipeline.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Amy Bernett, a security researcher on the OpenAI Codex security team, discusses the evolution and future trajectory of automated code reasoning and vulnerability remediation. Tracing the history from manual inspection to fuzzing, symbolic execution, and modern large language models (LLMs), Bernett highlights how frontier AI models are transforming defensive and offensive security, and what organizations must do to adapt to an AI-driven security pipeline.

### Key Topics
- **Evolution of Automated Vulnerability Discovery**: Moving through the dawn era of networked computing and faults, the rise of dumb-state fuzzing (adopted widely by organizations like Google), academic symbolic reasoning (which suffered from state explosion and lacked automated patching), and the current transition to LLM-powered code reasoning.
- **AI Cyber Challenge (AIxCC)**: Demonstration of modern capabilities through DARPA's two-year AI Cyber Challenge, where seven competing teams built systems capable of discovering and patching vulnerabilities, with all finalist teams successfully finding real zero-day flaws.
- **Shift in Security Pipeline and Vulnerability Types**: The integration of LLMs for pre-deployment code review, mass parallel reasoning across legacy software, and system hardening. As code generation accelerates, Bernett predicts security concerns will shift away from classic implementation bugs (e.g., SQL injection, buffer overflows) toward flawed policies, schemas, and specifications.
- **Emerging Supply Chain Risks**: Threats involving LLM-assisted sleeper agents posing as open-source contributors, poisoned third-party documentation/prompts, and malicious targeted libraries crafted to be picked up by autonomous development agents.
- **Autonomous Defender-Attacker Symbiosis**: Anticipating a future with agent swarms continuously monitoring, hardening, and patching vulnerabilities prior to public CVE disclosure, alongside OpenAI's Trusted Access for Cyber program.

### Technical Details
- **Historical Limitations vs. Modern LLMs**: Fuzzing was effective at crashing software but lacked context; symbolic execution converted code to mathematical forms to prove statements but failed to scale on complex real-world software due to state explosion and could not generate fixes. LLMs trained on internet-scale text generalize effectively to source code, enabling both fault detection and automated fix generation.
- **Remediation Bottleneck**: Bernett points out that while AI can surface hundreds of vulnerabilities rapidly, the primary bottleneck shifts to patch deployment velocity, testing pipelines, and dependency management.
- **Threat Modeling & Attack Economics**: Lowering the cost of vulnerability research reduces the defensive value of security through obscurity and forces organizations to recalculate threat models that previously relied on high attacker costs.
- **In-House Dependency Rewriting**: Organizations may eventually use AI agents to rewrite or maintain external dependencies in-house to mitigate supply chain tampering, relying on trusted golden sets and authoritative baselines.

### Takeaways
Defenders must aggressively adopt frontier reasoning models to match adversaries whose cost to discover exploits is dropping significantly. To operationalize code reasoning, organizations must improve testing infrastructure to patch at high velocity, harden systems against policy-level defects, establish trusted documentation baselines for agents, and deploy proactive defensive agent swarms.

talks.title: CYBERUK 2026 Tech Talk - How industrialised adversaries reveal CVEs weeks before disclosure
talks.teaser: Honeypot data shows scanning and exploit surges against edge devices often precede CVE disclosure by weeks.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that defenders usually start their clock at CVE disclosure, while attackers begin probing and exploiting flaws well before that point. The speaker presents data from a honeypot sensor grid of roughly 5,000 sensors in more than 80 countries, which records real-time scanning and exploitation aimed at internet-facing edge devices such as firewalls, VPNs and routers.

A 2025 study of 216 activity spikes found that half were followed by a CVE within three weeks and about 80% within six weeks. A later study covering around 103 days and roughly 148 million sessions across 18 vendors reported a median lead time of 11 days. Session-volume spikes gave the strongest signal, and when infrastructure growth in IP addresses rose alongside them, the pairing rate reached 71%, well above chance in a 10,000-permutation test. Scanning gave the earliest warnings, while brute force activity appeared later in the attack cycle. For two vendors, the warnings followed a shrinking countdown from 39 days to 3 days.

The speaker stresses that the signal is probabilistic and works as a decision support tool, not as a prediction of a specific CVE. It can give security teams time to brief leadership, stage patches and harden networks. The median IP-based lead time fell from 21 days in 2025 to 13 days in 2026, and the reason for that change was still under investigation.

talks.title: CYBERUK 2026 Technology Plenary - What will our future selves thank us for doing now?
talks.teaser: Panellists debate how governments and firms should share responsibility for long-term cyber resilience.
talks.summary:
The panel asks what decisions made now will be valued by future selves. The speakers start with lessons from the 9/11 Commission, which pointed to failures of imagination, policy, capabilities and management, and argue that similar gaps persist in how governments handle cyber risk. They frame attacks on critical infrastructure and the wider economy as national security issues, yet note that responsibility is often pushed onto boards and individual firms.

A speaker with government experience describes short political cycles, rotating civil servants and weak institutional memory, and explains that resilience spending is hard to justify because success looks like nothing happening. Another compares cyber risk to car safety, where manufacturers only adopted seat belts once minimum standards were required, and argues that vendors should share liability. Panellists agree that government should set a baseline and shape the conditions for decisions rather than direct technology markets, and they note that evidence on which controls work is thin.

To close, speakers call for courage and leadership that differs from management, a cross-sector national mission on cyber resilience, and preparation for a period when technology fails. Their message is that people must act themselves rather than wait for others to do it.

talks.title: CYBERUK 2026 Technology Plenary
talks.teaser: Surveys the shifting threat landscape and the long-term policy, technical and AI priorities for national cyber defense.
talks.summary:
This 10-minute CTO keynote at CYBERUK sets out how the speaker sees the threat environment changing. Commercial tools are reaching a wider range of actors, security products themselves have been a source of intrusions, software supply chain attacks are reaching six-digit scale, and AI is speeding up vulnerability discovery while being adopted in fragile ways. Mature defensive practice is spreading unevenly across the ecosystem.

Responses are split across short and long horizons. In the near term, a coordinated response to tactical vulnerability discoveries is planned during a forced correction of technical debt. Over the longer term, the speaker points to memory-safe languages, vendors providing hot patching so systems need not restart for every fix, and a legislative and market framework that rewards strong security. Other examples include passkeys and identity for agentic systems, privileged access workstations, post-quantum migration, cyber deception, vendor transparency, engineering resilience, and agentic AI for national defence. The talk also mentions a short story competition about future technology.

The closing message is to balance short-term incentives against long-term goals, act at a scale and pace not used before, and turn technical expertise and evidence into impact. The speaker warns that consumer robotics is repeating vulnerabilities from the last twenty years, and that delay makes the problem compound.

talks.title: Stuart Mckenzie, MD, Mandiant Consulting in conversation with Darragh M, Director of Comms, NCSC
talks.teaser: Traces how attackers have moved from phishing to edge device exploits and stolen credentials, and what defenders should fix.
talks.summary:
In this CYBERUK interview, Stuart Mckenzie of Mandiant Consulting, part of Google Cloud, describes how threat actors have changed their approach. Exploiting vulnerabilities has overtaken phishing as the most common initial attack vector. Last year, four of the top five exploited vulnerabilities were in edge devices, which rarely have much security tooling or logging. Attackers can sit on these devices and then use tools already present in the environment. Stolen credentials ranked second, which he links to weak multi-factor authentication and SMS-based second factors.

He said financial services is the most targeted sector, followed by consulting firms, government and healthcare, though this reflects Mandiant's own investigations. Dwell time has fallen from 99 days when he joined in 2016 to 11 days now, and was 10 days globally last year. Fifty-seven percent of notifications to affected organisations came from an external party. He separated nation-state groups, including a Chinese nexus group showing interest in critical national infrastructure, from financially motivated criminals. He noted that North Korean groups target both.

His main advice was to get the basics right: patch and vulnerability management, knowing which firmware and devices are in use, and stronger phishing-resistant authentication. Each step makes intrusion harder and creates detection points, such as failed logins or unusual east-west movement. He warned that attackers will adapt as defences improve, so organisations need continuous monitoring.

talks.title: Palo Alto Networks: Transforming resilience. Countering threats.
talks.teaser: Looks at UK cyber resilience amid tool sprawl and AI-driven threats, with NCSC's assessment framework as a starting point.
talks.summary:
This short session, part of the CYBERUK online programme, looks at how approaches to cyber resilience and threat response are changing in the UK. It opens with the threat picture: the NCSC views the UK as underprepared for the current environment, with geopolitical tensions, nation states targeting the UK, and extortion aimed at critical national infrastructure. Legacy systems, complex supply chains and an evolving regulatory landscape add to the difficulty.

The discussion then turns to resilience and the strain of fragmented technology. Research by Palo Alto Networks and IBM is cited, finding that the average organisation runs more than 83 security tools from almost 30 vendors. Among executives surveyed, 52% said tooling complexity was getting in the way of managing cyber threats. The speakers also describe how AI gives attackers more speed, scale and sophistication, and how a malware market of access brokers, as-a-service tools and affiliates lowers attacker costs while widening the opportunity. The effects on operations, service delivery and reputation are noted.

For practical steps, the NCSC Cyber Assessment Framework is presented as a sound starting point, covering governance, protection of assets and the ability to respond to incidents. Security culture and modelling how relevant threat actors would behave, so that defences can be tested, are highlighted as further needs. A 2025 global incident response report is cited, in which 86% of major incidents caused operational impact, financial loss, reputational loss or outages. The session closes by calling for lessons from current incidents, the use of AI and automation in connected platforms so small teams can do more, and secure by design as a recurring theme.

talks.title: Securing the future
talks.teaser: Covers foreign influence threats to elections and the Paris Olympics, plus how AI could help defenders keep pace.
talks.summary:
The interview looks at how Microsoft's Threat Analysis Center works with sister teams to protect democratic processes worldwide. Examples include an account protection program, an industry accord on preventing malicious AI use such as deepfakes in elections, and monitoring of influence activity linked to Russia, Iran and China. The guest stresses that trust in elections depends on verifiable results and on protecting election workers and institutions.

Looking ahead to the Paris Olympics, the guest expects Russia to target the International Olympic Committee and the French government, possibly by discrediting institutions or spreading false safety conspiracies about athletes. Iran was described as relying mainly on influence and claims of cyber attacks rather than many successful intrusions. Russia was said to combine hack-and-leak operations with influence work, with its war in Ukraine producing a multi-year cyber conflict. China's Volt Typhoon activity was described as moving beyond espionage toward infrastructure access, and its covert social media account building as a new development.

On AI, the guest argues that defenders must succeed every day while attackers need only one opening, so the gap has to be closed with more capacity. Microsoft's Security Copilot is presented as a way to speed detection, analysis and triage so analysts can focus on the most sophisticated attacks. The guest is optimistic this could shift the balance, and the interview closes on the value of public-private partnership at Cyber UK.

talks.title: The biggest hack ever?
talks.teaser: An interview explores how laundering networks enable cybercrime cash-outs, crypto tracing limits, and North Korea's cross-border fund moves.
talks.summary:
The conversation continues a Cyber UK thread tied to investigative work for an upcoming book on money laundering and how technology shapes criminal finance. The guest argues that cybercrime, ransomware, and other profitable intrusions only work when enabler networks wash proceeds so money survives arrest and conviction, linking the same machinery to cartels and other organized crime.

Cryptocurrency matters because public blockchains expose transaction paths, yet law enforcement still struggles to freeze and recover funds once flows are understood. On North Korea, the discussion treats alleged state-backed hacking as revenue under sanctions, describing stolen crypto as liquid capital moved worldwide for bribes and sensitive purchases rather than hoarded at home.

A featured bank compromise in India shows jurisdictional leverage: cash extracted through ATMs across many countries in a short window, coordinated digitally, while police face language and cooperation delays. The takeaway is that following money and cross-border cash-out tactics is as central to the cybercrime picture as the hacks themselves.

talks.title: Responding to an Evolving Threat Picture
talks.teaser: A US cyber official discusses shifting defense responsibility, resilience investment, partnerships and information sharing.
talks.summary:
In this CYBERUK Online interview, NCSC chief executive Felicity Oswald speaks with US cyber official Harry Koker about how the United States approaches evolving cyber threats. Koker describes two shifts in the national cyber strategy: moving the duty of defending cyberspace away from end users and toward the most capable actors, including federal agencies and large technology firms, and encouraging strategic investment in cyber resilience. Building security in from the outset, he argues, is cheaper and more effective than adding it later.

Koker stresses that threats will keep changing and that the public should understand them without being frightened, since cyber risks can hit as hard as traditional security threats even when unseen. No government can succeed alone, he says, so the approach relies on state, local, tribal and territorial governments, the private sector and allies such as the Five Eyes. On keeping an edge, he says it means being bold, never complacent, and assuming adversaries hold the same offensive capabilities the US has, so defenses must match them.

Looking ahead, he says success in the coming decade will depend on information sharing at the speed, scale and scope that missions require, across borders as well as between public and private sectors. He recalls sharing information before Russia's invasion of Ukraine and notes that sources and methods, more than the information itself, most need protecting. The closing point is that information only matters when it is put to use promptly.

talks.title: CYBERUK 2024: ‘Future Threat’ with the Deputy Director, Incident Management at the NCSC
talks.teaser: An NCSC incident leader surveys how AI, criminal ecosystems and cyber insurance shape the UK threat landscape.
talks.summary:
This interview with the NCSC's deputy director for incident management opens with emerging technologies such as quantum and AI. The speaker argues that adversaries are pursuing the same tools, so defenders need to use AI to protect their digital footprint and stay one step ahead of attackers.

The conversation then turns to the criminal threat. Commercial tools have lowered the barrier to entry, so people with little technical skill can launch attacks. Criminal groups also now operate as ecosystems, with some gaining initial network access, others building ransomware, and others handling victims' negotiations and payments. Ransomware as a service is described as a way for a developed strain to reach groups that could never have built it themselves.

On cyber insurance, the speaker says insured organisations tend to be better prepared, because buying cover usually means having a response plan and passing baseline security checks. The NCSC works with insurers to raise those baselines. The early warning service is presented as a free sign-up that pulls together commercial feeds, partner reporting and internal findings to get urgent alerts to the right people. The interview closes by inviting listeners to an event in May on future technology.

talks.title: CYBERUK 2024: ‘Future Ready’ with the Deputy Director, Critical National Infrastructure at the NCSC
talks.teaser: An NCSC interview on securing critical national infrastructure as AI and net zero technologies reshape resilience and risk.
talks.summary:
This short interview looks at how new technologies, including AI, affect the security of critical national infrastructure. The guest explains that a technology which starts out as emerging can become critical over time, much as the internet did, so the priority is understanding the risks each new tool brings while still embracing the opportunities it offers the wider economy. Resilience, meaning how essential services would keep running without a given technology, is presented as a central concern.

On the changing threat picture, the guest points to several alerts the NCSC has issued over the past year about evolving threats. Organisations at every level are urged to understand the threats and to plan how they would prevent and respond to incidents. Rehearsing with the board what the organisation would do after a cyber attack is described as a way to achieve a much better response.

The discussion then turns to net zero. Energy is used as an example: new ways of producing power bring new risks, and while older infrastructure has to have cyber security retrofitted, new providers give an opportunity to build protection in from the start. The closing advice is to design systems to be secure by design from day one. The guest ends by encouraging attendance at CYBERUK in May as a place to meet partners and collaborators.

talks.title: CYBERUK 2024: ‘Future Ready’ with the Deputy Director, Cyber Growth at the NCSC
talks.teaser: A guest from the NCSC discusses building future-ready cyber skills, diversity, research and startups in the UK.
talks.summary:
In this pre-event interview ahead of CYBERUK, Chris, the NCSC's Deputy Director for Cyber Growth, argues that many of the sector's problems start with technology that is insecure by default. He says the ecosystem should aim for security by design, so that products are made safe from the outset instead of being patched later.

On skills, he says the main gap is people who truly understand how technology works, noting that much of today's internet still rests on standards dating from the 1970s. He points to the Cyber First programme, which runs outside the school curriculum, as a route into the field. He reports that applications from girls rose to around 40% this year and from ethnic minority applicants to over 50%, a result he credits to early school outreach, a girls' competition and summer courses. On research, he says the academic centres of excellence grew from about nine universities a decade ago to 19, supported by four research institutes. On innovation, the NCSC's startup programme, now around seven years old, has seen over 60 companies come through, raising about 500 million and creating 1600 jobs.

He closes by recommending CYBERUK in May as a place to meet industry and academia and learn from peers.

talks.title: CYBERUK 2024: ‘Future Tech’ with the Director of National Resilience & Future Technology at the NCSC
talks.teaser: NCSC leader discusses AI risks and opportunities, quantum-safe cryptography and building security into technology from the start.
talks.summary:
The interview opens with the future of cyber security in an AI-driven world. The interviewee says the NCSC has researched AI and machine learning for some time, and that recent government attention, including the Prime Minister's AI summit, has put secure design for AI in a prominent place. The agency has since published guidance on building secure AI systems and on deploying them on networks. He argues that AI could also help defenders, for example by improving the accuracy of reports and data and of threat detection and response, but that the cyber security risks from these systems must be treated with clear eyes.

On post-quantum cryptography, the NCSC's 2020 white paper described the threat that future, far more capable quantum computers could pose to the public cryptography that protects data in transit, along with post-quantum solutions. In 2023 the agency issued guidance to organisations on what they need to start doing now. Although the threat is still some way off, he stresses that businesses should engage with the issue early.

Turning to secure foundations, he names two main challenges: the skills and capabilities needed to build security in from the outset, and market incentives. Vendors need reasons to invest in the right technologies, and customers need to create demand, so that the economic case for security holds across a product's whole life cycle. Closing the interview, he describes CYBERUK in the West Midlands as a rare mix of experts, policymakers, international delegates, industry and academia, and recommends attending.

talks.title: CYBERUK 2023 - Stream B, Session 1, The future belongs to those who prepare for it today
talks.teaser: Officials from several countries discuss preparing for future cyber threats through basics, partnerships and a skilled workforce.
talks.summary:
A panel of officials from New Zealand, the United States and the United Kingdom discusses whether organisations can prepare for the future of cyber threats, and what that preparation should look like. The New Zealand speaker describes a blurring between state and criminal activity, with about a third of incidents reported to their national agency left unattributed, and commercial tools giving criminals access to sophisticated capability. The US speaker argues that preparedness depends less on tracking each threat and more on processes, trusted partnerships, asset discovery, patch management and a plan that can adapt when an adversary behaves unexpectedly.

The UK National Crime Agency speaker frames the goal as becoming a survivor rather than a victim, noting that ransomware relies on leverage over encrypted data and that doing the basics well removes much of that power. The panel expects adversaries to target managed service providers to reach many victims at once, and to reuse techniques learned from past incidents, including supply chain compromises and rapid exploitation of newly disclosed flaws. The Cabinet Office speaker stresses building security in from the start of technology and supply chains, and points to a shortage of 14 000 skilled experts in the UK.

Later, the panellists discuss government's role in sharing threat context with industry, and the risk of hidden dependencies on unprotected systems created by technical debt. They close on workforce resilience and secure by design as ways to reduce the need for scarce expertise. The practical message is to keep the basics current, build partnerships before a crisis, and plan for change.

talks.teaser: Security researchers investigate CYBERUK 2023 and analyze defensive countermeasures.
talks.summary:
### Overview
This session represents the final plenary and closing proceedings of CYBERUK 2023, hosted in Belfast, Northern Ireland, and led by National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) CEO Lindy Cameron. The event features an excerpted interview with tech pioneer Hermann Hauser, a speculative dystopian video depicting an overwhelmed cyber ecosystem in 2033, an expert panel titled 'Fixing the Foundations', the Cyber Den startup pitch competition awards, and formal closing remarks reflecting on the conference and announcing Birmingham as the host city for CYBERUK 2024.

### Key Topics
- **Fixing the Foundations & Memory Safety:** The session emphasizes moving past reactive patching to embed security directly into fundamental hardware and software design, specifically tackling long-standing memory safety issues.
- **Market Pull vs. Vendor Push:** Panelists debate the economic and supply chain barriers to adopting secure-by-design architectures, noting that creating widespread commercial demand across large industries is essential to drive unit costs down.
- **Securing 'Hard Tech' and Global Supply Chains:** A significant portion of the discussion addresses heavy engineering, defense, nuclear, and aerospace sectors, where massive digitization and multinational supply chains vastly expand attack surfaces.
- **Innovation and Startup Ecosystem:** Highlighting early-stage innovators addressing practical problems through the Cyber Den competition and showcasing Northern Ireland's cyber ecosystem.

### Technical Details
- **Foundational Architecture and Memory Safety:** Panelists highlighted that approximately 70% of exploitable vulnerabilities originate from memory safety flaws such as buffer overflows. Discussion focused on the UKRI-supported Digital Security by Design (DSbD) program and Arm's prototype Morello chip, which incorporates CHERI (Capability Hardware Enhanced RISC Instructions) technology developed by the University of Cambridge and SRI.
- **Formally Verified Software:** Hauser noted proof theory achievements in operating systems, highlighting seL4 as a proven-correct microkernel, contrasting it with the broader challenge of securing the estimated three trillion lines of code written over the last two decades.
- **Hard Tech Digitization:** Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) and jet engines involve extensive IT integration, including 100,000-core computing clusters for simulation, digital twinning, IoT pallet tracking, and the full codification of manufacturing methods across millions of parts (e.g., 30 million codified parts in an SMR and 36,000 components in a jet engine). This codification risks theft of proprietary manufacturing techniques across tiered global suppliers.
- **Cyber Den Technologies:** Pitch finalists included Visible (managing digital footprints), Sightec/Sight Hop (low-latency hardware-enforced encryption for high-speed data links), and the winning startup ITUS Secure Technologies (aggregating third-party risk assessments to enable cyber insurance underwriting).

### Takeaways
- **Demand Generation Over Pure Technology Push:** Proving secure hardware concepts requires building multi-industry demand—combining defense, telecommunications, and hyperscalers—to make secure chips economically viable for consumer hardware.
- **Broader Sector Engagement:** The cybersecurity community must actively engage hard tech, heavy engineering, and manufacturing CIOs rather than remaining an isolated deep-tech echo chamber.
- **Proactive Implementation:** Organizations cannot wait for future crises or slow regulatory mandates; requirements for secure-by-design capabilities must be written into systems procured today for deployment in the 2030s.

The Belfast plenary frames CYBER UK 2023 around securing an open, resilient digital future. NCSC chief Lindy Cameron reviews a year of nationally significant incidents, stresses cyber resilience after Russia’s war on Ukraine, and points to breach-survey figures showing many UK businesses and charities hit by often basic hygiene gaps. She highlights Cyber Essentials, a new Cyber Advisor scheme for smaller organizations, and long-horizon risks in AI, semiconductors, quantum cryptography, 6G and telecoms, plus concerns over commercial cyber capability proliferation and China’s technology ambitions.

Cabinet Office minister Oliver Dowden describes a more dangerous threat picture—state actors, ransomware at national-security scale, and Russian-aligned groups targeting critical national infrastructure—and announces GovAssure for government departments, a live NCSC CNI alert, and 2025 resilience targets with possible regulatory expansion for CNI operators. Google’s Nick Godfrey argues cloud migration, secure-by-default design, AI-assisted defenses, and partnership are essential. White House acting National Cyber Director Kemba Walden presents the U.S. strategy’s affirmative vision: rebalance who bears cyber risk and build ecosystems that are defensible and resilient by design.

A panel with UK, U.S., and Singapore officials compares integrated-review priorities, Ukraine takeaways (people, offense limits, narratives, supply chains), Indo-Pacific sanctions and alertness, and interoperability as an enabler of digital trade. Practitioners should hear a coordinated push to invest in resilience now, treat baseline hygiene as economic necessity, and align internationally on responsibility and secure foundations before emerging tech hardens into legacy risk.

## Overview
James Stewart interviews Viscount Camrose, Minister for AI and Intellectual Property at DSIT (Department of Science Innovation and Technology) with responsibility for cyber security, at CYBERUK 2023 in Belfast. The conversation covers government cyber security priorities, the health of the UK cyber ecosystem, and emerging threats from artificial intelligence.

## Event Context
The conference drew over 2,000 attendees to Belfast. DSIT announced £300 million in investment in the cyber security sector this year, reflecting significant sector growth that contributes to the broader UK economy.

## DSIT Cyber Security Priorities
Camrose outlined three main priorities:

1. **Protecting at Source and at Scale**: Connected devices should meet minimum online safety standards that consumers can understand and compare. The government must operate agilely and at scale to respond to emerging technologies, such as AI, which has rapidly moved into the spotlight.

2. **Managing Residual Risk**: Both large and small organizations must understand and manage their own risks. A successful attack on critical national infrastructure—such as a health system or utility—could cost approximately 1.5% of national GDP, representing an absolute crisis to avoid. Smaller organizations and charities must also be cyber-aware to protect their own assets and those of their customers and donors.

3. **Building a Talent Pipeline**: Camrose emphasized encouraging young people into cyber security careers through programs like CyberFirst, noting encouraging engagement during his time in Belfast.

## AI and Cyber Security Implications
Camrose discussed how AI disrupts the traditional equilibrium between cyber attack and defense. Historically, defense held a slight advantage except for the human factor. AI strengthens defense by improving pattern detection and hardware Trojan identification, but simultaneously strengthens attack capabilities. Large language models, particularly ChatGPT, excel at deceiving humans into believing they are human themselves. A specific concern is that LLMs can generate sophisticated spear-phishing and mass phishing emails at scale, representing an emerging threat that requires close monitoring to understand how it shifts the attack-defense balance.

## Takeaways
The government recognizes cyber security as critical national infrastructure requiring significant investment and attention. Smaller organizations lag in cyber awareness and require targeted support. The rapid advancement of AI presents both defensive opportunities and offensive risks that demand ongoing vigilance and agile policy responses.

talks.title: Lindy Cameron interviews Jen Easterly at CYBERUK 2023.
talks.teaser: Covers transatlantic cyber collaboration, secure-by-design duties and societal resilience after a major pipeline attack.
talks.summary:
Recorded in Belfast at CYBERUK 2023, this short interview pairs the head of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre with a leader from a close US partner agency. The two reflect on their first conference day, the value of international collaboration, and nearly two years of joint work on advisories and products, including support for Ukraine.

The conversation breaks cyber responsibility into layers. Individuals should adopt basics such as multi-factor authentication, boards and executives must treat cyber risk as a matter of governance, and technology makers should build products that are secure by design and secure by default instead of prioritising speed, cost and features. Joint guidance matters because good practice travels between countries, and holding vendors to account is more powerful when governments act together. Ransomware is acknowledged as a hard problem where some progress is starting to appear.

The closing part turns to resilience, using a 2021 pipeline intrusion in the United States that caused fuel shortages along the Eastern Seaboard for several days even though operational technology was not affected. The lesson drawn is that societies cannot prevent every attack, so they need to respond calmly, recover and reduce risk rather than panic. Lessons from Ukraine reinforce that point, and the interview ends with thanks to the guests.

talks.title: Google: From information sharing to building a collective view of intelligence
talks.teaser: Explains why threat data sharing falls short and how a collective view of intelligence can make it more actionable.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that information sharing has earned a poor reputation because it is often treated as a vague, easy fix. The speaker names three recurring shortcomings: shared data is usually unverified and lacks context, exchanges drift away from ground truth without settling what should be shared, and sharing efforts lose sight of the goal of improving security.

The speaker separates raw information, which lacks context and validity, from intelligence, which is defined by actionability and starts from the problems network defenders face. A plain list of bad indicators is contrasted with a list of indicators tied to high-risk activity active in an organization's sector over six months. Collection is the second component: different organizations see different parts of the threat landscape, so the aim is to combine complementary perspectives rather than rank institutions against each other, with collection tied to stakeholder requirements. The speaker also cites how one platform's visibility gains from frontline incident response observations.

The final component is people. Sharing initiatives packed with senior names lose momentum if they do not address practitioners' tangible problems, so successful ones work alongside stakeholders and build products around their challenges within the intelligence life cycle. The takeaway is to move from simply exchanging information toward building a collective view of intelligence that lets defenders take decisive action.

talks.summary:
# Overview
In this talk, representatives from Nominet Cyber discuss the critical role of Protective DNS (PDNS) in securing public infrastructure and building a resilient digital future. Based in Oxford in the UK, Nominet Cyber has a team of approximately 70 people and operates Protective DNS services on behalf of the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) in the UK and the Australian Cyber Security Centre (ACSC). The service is designed to mitigate online disruptions for public sector bodies, enabling innovation and growth across the digital economy.

# Key Topics
- **Protective DNS (PDNS) Operation and Reach**: Nominet delivers PDNS across the vast majority of the UK public sector, ranging from central and local government to healthcare and emergency services. The service aims to protect organizations from the majority of cyber threats online, aligning with the ethos of the Active Cyber Defence program.
- **Threat Intelligence and Decision-Making**: The service relies on threat intelligence to determine what domain activity should or should not be blocked, separating malicious traffic from benign requests to prevent attacks such as phishing.
- **Customer Experience and Awareness**: Operating the service involves supporting customer interactions across the lifetime of use—from onboarding on day one onward—alongside raising awareness through webinars, communications, and industry events such as CyberUK.
- **Cybersecurity Mindset and Public-Private Collaboration**: Building collective resilience requires embedding cybersecurity best practices and online safety into education and professional training early on, as well as fostering non-profit-driven collaboration between the public and private sectors.

# Technical Details
- **Architecture and Scale**: The PDNS platform operates at national scale, capable of protecting entire governments or nations by intercepting and mitigating cyber threats at the DNS level.
- **Threat Mitigation**: The team conducts threat research and leverages threat intelligence to detect and mitigate malicious activity—such as phishing campaigns and cyberattacks—blocking threats before they disrupt critical citizen-facing operations.
- **Operational Structure**: The team is split into two primary operational areas: customer onboarding and lifetime relationship management for public sector entities, and threat intelligence research that informs real-time blocking and filtering rules.

# Takeaways
- **Quiet and Effective Protection**: PDNS functions with minimal fuss and disruption, providing verifiable evidence of blocked malicious threats across critical infrastructure like healthcare and emergency response.
- **Need for Greater Public Benefit Initiatives**: Speakers highlighted the need for expanded government intervention under active cyber defence programs and encouraged public and private sector entities to collaborate beyond pure profit motivations to build collective resilience.
- **Foundational Education**: Embedding online safety into foundational education and professional training ensures individuals maintain a security-oriented mindset both at work and in their personal lives.

They also value exposure to the wider ecosystem, chances to present to large audiences, and corporate and public sector trials.

Both speakers stress that the cyber ecosystem needs soft skills alongside technical knowledge, such as explaining complex challenges, linking big and small firms, and bringing public and private sectors closer together. They present events like CYBERUK, held in Belfast, as places for training, networking and sharing innovation. For a practitioner weighing a startup path, the takeaway is that the programme offers a route to mentors, trials and a direct channel between government problems and the people building products to solve them.

The director of CISA, unable to attend in person, delivered prerecorded remarks to open a panel on supply chain security. Using the time allotted, the speaker argues that imagination should underpin cyber defense over the coming decade. The remarks open with a run of notable historical events from May 11, then turn to the September 11 attacks, where a commission co-chair described the failure as one of imagination as well as policy, management and capability.

The speaker recalls a 2007 deployment to Baghdad, where a small team built a regional gateway that enriched and correlated collection data so that bomb-making networks could be identified within hours rather than weeks. The same year brought the first iPhone, the launch of GitHub and Android, and the early growth of Twitter. The central question posed is who will create the key technologies of the future, set the rules for their use, secure them and train the talent to build them. Examples include 5G telecom standards, facial recognition, quantum computing, artificial intelligence, the openness of the internet and privacy by design for smart cities.

The speaker's answer is that these outcomes depend on investing in alliances, people and global standards grounded in shared democratic values. Doing so would make secure and resilient software, systems, networks and supply chains the norm, so that a major intrusion or a severe zero-day vulnerability becomes the exception. Conferences such as CYBERUK are presented as places where those connections and ideas are formed.

talks.title: CYBERUK TV: Director of the New Zealand NCSC Lisa Fong speaks to the NCSC’s James Stewart
talks.teaser: A New Zealand cyber agency director explains how it protects critical infrastructure, tackles rising threats and builds diversity.
talks.summary:
In this CYBERUK interview, the UK NCSC's communications director talks with Lisa Fong, head of New Zealand's national cyber security centre, about protecting critical national infrastructure. Fong outlines the agency's security information exchanges, which bring energy and banking organisations into trusted environments to share what they observe and receive threat indicators. She also describes a voluntary code issued jointly with the control systems exchange and exercises run with the national grid provider.

On threats, Fong reports that incidents have risen, with non-state actors roughly doubling as sophisticated tools reach criminal groups. Non-attributed activity is also up, making it hard to tell actors apart in the early stages of compromise. She points to rapid exploitation of vulnerabilities, global supply chains that leave everyone exposed, and ransomware combined with pressure through the media. She recalls the Waikato health incident, where five hospitals shut down and staff worked with pen and paper, and says the episode helped leaders treat cyber risk as a strategic and operational concern.

The closing section covers workforce diversity. Fong says targets helped the agency meet its gender pay gap goal and a senior women leadership quota. Next priorities are developing technical leaders from within rather than hiring from outside, encouraging women to stay in STEM study through scholarships for Māori and Pacific students, running a graduate programme, and backing staff networks for gender, neurodiversity and ethnic identity.

talks.title: Safe CEO
talks.teaser: Explains how unified APIs and predictive models turn fragmented security telemetry into breach likelihood and dollar risk for leaders.
talks.summary:
Organizations still struggle to express cyber risk in terms executives understand. The discussion opens with three structural gaps: security tooling stays siloed across endpoints, applications, and cloud, operations remain largely reactive, and teams lack a single, credible view of posture that maps to business outcomes. Even large security budgets leave leadership worried because scores and traffic-light ratings substitute for measurable risk.

The Safe Security platform is described as API-first aggregation across people, process, and technology, feeding analytics akin to financial predictive models. Bayesian and data-science approaches estimate ransomware probability from findings across connected tools and translate exposure into likelihood and monetary impact, co-developed with MIT research rather than subjective red-amber-green judgments.

BT’s Eagle Eye managed security proposition integrates Safe to add risk context to real-time policy and remediation decisions. Customers gain visualization of evolving posture while automated workflows weigh threat impact against organizational appetite. Practitioners should take away that unifying external signals with quantified, business-aligned metrics can prioritize remediation and support automated choices without treating risk as an opaque technical sidebar.

talks.title: Leonardo Cyber Advantage
talks.teaser: Cyber resilience, unified risk reporting, and OT-aware monitoring are positioned as enablers for UK digitization and 5G-driven change.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens on a tension facing UK industry: digital transformation and 5G will move vast data volumes and enable smart manufacturing, yet security must accelerate that change rather than block it. Without embedded protection, systems ship with unacceptable risk, or gatekeepers halt programs and business value never materializes.

Two responses are outlined. Security solutions should align business and security outcomes—for example, in time-critical factory flows, late-added encryption can add latency, whereas secure-by-design choices such as lower-latency layer-two cryptography can preserve both aims. Separately, risk management should give decision makers consistent insight instead of treating cyber, financial, OT, and enterprise IT risks in silos, recognizing that frameworks are easy to document but hard to operationalize.

Leonardo’s Cyber Advantage family is described through three offerings: NCSC-certified resilience consulting for architecture and risk across defence, government, and national infrastructure; monitoring that establishes “normal” behavior on OT and enterprise networks; and cyber ranges that stand up combined IT/OT training at proportional fidelity. Cyber resilience is framed as planning for eventual compromise while still prioritizing outcomes—illustrated by an autonomous bus favoring passenger safety over schedule when navigation is attacked—with similar thinking applied to programs such as future combat air and national 5G rollout.

talks.title: PA Cyber Transformation
talks.teaser: UK cyber transformation leadership paints digital trust for citizens and three pillars for weaving security into digital growth.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with a fictional day in the life of Sam, a remote worker whose home, employer, bank, supermarket, and travel services share data through interconnected cloud and smart devices. Quantum-resistant encryption, proactive sensor alerts, and automated scheduling illustrate a world built on complete digital trust between people and institutions.

The narrative shifts from that aspirational picture to what organizations must do to reach it safely. Growth driven by technology only works if security is woven into how services are delivered. The speaker frames cyber transformation as uniting secure-by-design systems, processes that make compliance the easy path, and people who understand cyber risk in business terms.

Board and working-level staff are urged to see security as enabling better digital service delivery, not blocking it. Redesigned compliance processes can give teams ownership, with examples cited from financial services and government. With those foundations, systems should match organizational risk appetite, adapt as threats change, and support continuous improvement as technology evolves.

talks.title: Ministerial Address
talks.teaser: A UK Home Secretary sets out government priorities on ransomware, state threats and a review of the Computer Misuse Act.
talks.summary:
The Home Secretary addresses an NCSC online event and frames cyber security as a core part of the homeland security mission, thanking NCSC staff for work protecting the country. The speaker names hostile states, organised criminals and terrorists as threats and cites an estimated 1.7 million cyber-dependent crimes against adults in England and Wales in the year to September 2020.

Ransomware gets particular attention. The speaker says NCSC figures show rising ransomware incidents, with criminals researching targets to demand larger extortion payments. The government's stance is against paying ransoms, since payment does not guarantee recovery, stop future attacks or prevent leaks, and tends to encourage more criminality. Organisations are urged to contact the NCSC and law enforcement early, understand how an incident would affect them over time, and rehearse their responses. Interior ministers from the Five Eyes group have pledged joint action against ransomware.

The speaker also cites the SolarWinds compromise and an attack on US fuel pipelines as examples of capable state and criminal operations. Funding for police cyber capability, the National Cyber Force and cyber resilience centres is outlined, along with work on child sexual abuse enforcement. The talk closes by announcing a formal review of the Computer Misuse Act, with a call for information this year, and asking public and private sector participants to share honest views.

talks.title: How to make a Difference Locally
talks.teaser: A panel of regional cyber cluster leaders explains how local groups build skills, innovation and growth across the UK.
talks.summary:
A panel of cluster leaders explains how regional cyber clusters operate. Phil Jackman from Cyber North in the north-east of England, Claire Johnson from the women in cyber cluster in Cyber Wales and Kiera Mitchell from the Scotland cluster describe clusters as a way to bring academia, commercial providers and practitioners together into one regional voice. Each cluster differs; Wales, for example, runs north and south groups alongside subject clusters for industrial control, capture the flag and education.

On growth, Kiera describes passing funding and programme news to small firms that lack time to track it, and arranging roundtables with Scottish government procurement staff. Phil describes raising the region's profile, closing the gap between graduates and employer needs, and building an innovation centre with Newcastle University to turn ideas into businesses. Claire covers lunch-and-learn sessions where industry staff teach students, support for overseas firms relocating, and retraining routes into the sector. Diversity recurs throughout, from neurodiverse people and veterans to school outreach.

The closing remarks focus on structure. Clusters have largely run on volunteer time or sponsorship, so the UK Cyber Cluster Collaboration is being set up to route government funding to regional groups and represent them nationally. Listeners are directed to the Cyber Exchange website to find a local cluster, and the panel urges businesses from outside cyber, which rely on security, to get involved. Stereotyped imagery, the panel argues, puts many people off the field.

talks.title: Preparing the UK for a Secure Future in Quantum Technology
talks.teaser: Covers the UK's quantum technology ecosystem, quantum-safe cryptography timelines, trusted research and investment security.
talks.summary:
The session, from the National Cyber Security Centre, opens with an overview of the UK's quantum technology programmes, including the national quantum computing centre and its research hubs. It explains that large-scale quantum computers able to break today's public key cryptography are still likely at least a decade away, so the threat is serious but not immediate. The cryptography section explains that current public key systems rely on integer factorisation and discrete logarithms, which a large quantum computer could solve. NIST is drafting quantum-safe replacements, and most organisations are advised to wait for standards-compliant products, while those protecting long-lived data should start planning their transition now.

The trusted research segment, a joint product from CPNI and NCSC, addresses how universities and companies can protect sensitive research and staff from hostile intent. Recommended steps include simple open-source due diligence on collaboration partners, checking for conflicts of interest, controlling access to systems and considering reputational risk. The aim is to protect intellectual property without blocking international collaboration.

The final section covers the National Security and Investment Bill, which names quantum as one of 17 sectors where certain acquisitions need notification and clearance. It also introduces secure innovation guidance aimed at early-stage companies and venture investors, covering basics from password security to safe internet connection and planning for security as a company scales. The session closed with links to NCSC quantum white papers and the trusted research guidance.

talks.title: Understanding Cyber Crises
talks.teaser: Explains why cyber crises behave like transboundary crises and which management challenges follow for national responders.
talks.summary:
Sarah Bachman, a researcher at Stockholm University, presents her study on how cyber crises unfold in national settings. She argues that large-scale cyber crises are under-studied and under-theorised, and proposes treating them as transboundary crises that cut across political, functional and time boundaries. Her working definition covers IT disruptions that threaten key services or critical infrastructure with publicly visible consequences, whatever the cause.

The talk walks through seven crisis management task domains: detection, sense making, decision making, coordination, meaning making and communication, and termination. For each, she sets out what transboundary crisis literature predicts and then the challenges raised in her interviews with responders. Examples include fragmented and contradictory technical information, unclear ownership of decisions, competing public narratives and media-driven panic, and a slow-burning tail that makes it hard to tell when an incident is over. A road crash analogy, with ambulances, traffic diversion and investigations running at once, illustrates why coordination is so difficult.

For practitioners, she suggests that national arrangements need rapid access to scarce technical expertise, room for improvised and pragmatic responses, trust-based relationships built before a crisis, fast delivery of clear public advice, and staff who can bridge agencies, companies and technical and political levels. She also points to distributed sense making, networked coordination, surge capacity and formal scaling procedures as mechanisms worth building.

talks.title: Industry Discuss Their Experiences and Benefits of Being Part of the NCSC’s CyberFirst Programme
talks.teaser: Industry panellists describe how their organisations took part in the NCSC's CyberFirst programme and what it gave them.
talks.summary:
A panel of industry representatives from Morgan Stanley, Lloyd's Banking Group, Allstate, IBM, BT and Tesco explains how their organisations have taken part in CyberFirst, the NCSC programme for finding and nurturing people for cyber security careers. Chris Ensor, the NCSC's deputy director for cyber growth, introduces the scheme, which began as a bursary for students heading to university and later added competitions and courses to widen the pool of applicants.

Panellists describe what their firms gained. IBM said bursary students arrived familiar with security vetting and classified-area rules, and that moving between government and industry placements made them attractive hires. Lloyd's ran ten summer placements, rotating students across teams, and the students helped automate some processes. BT linked the scheme to its graduate programme, letting former placement students skip the online tests and video interviews. Allstate recalled two early bursary students who made a strong impression. Morgan Stanley and Tesco hosted girls' competitions to address gender balance, and Tesco noted that parents and teachers were glad to see a retailer involved.

The discussion closed on regional reach. Panellists suggested running regional semi-finals, supplying content for teachers, and building local education networks, since students often drift away from technology around age 14 or 15. For firms not yet ready to hire, they recommended smaller steps such as careers talks, role models and roundtables. The core message was that involvement at any scale helps build the talent pipeline.

talks.title: Palo Alto Networks: Building a Cyber Ecosystem
talks.teaser: Argues that cyber ecosystems need visibility, data correlation and automation to keep pace with cloud growth and alert volumes.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why security ecosystems have to change. Greg Day, chief security officer at Palo Alto Networks, opens with the upheaval of the pandemic, when rapid moves to remote work and cloud services arrived alongside existing data protection duties and Brexit-related rule changes. He argues that growing data volumes and alert floods, set against shrinking response windows, create a squeeze he calls the cyber time paradox.

He sets out three capabilities an ecosystem needs. Visibility means knowing on-premises, cloud, SaaS and shadow IT assets, plus the external attack surface. Data correlation normalizes alerts into a common structure, maps them to frameworks such as MITRE ATT&CK and links related behaviours, with machine learning helping to spot new attacks. Response uses automation for routine steps such as blocking traffic or notifying senders, freeing scarce analysts for complex threats. He cites Unit 42 research showing many cloud breaches stem from poor access controls, and presents zero trust as a strategy rather than a product, applying minimum access rights and, in DevOps pipelines, assigning rights dynamically before release.

To close, he gives three takeaways: visibility underpins risk management and zero trust, so the basics such as access control must be right; legacy systems should be brought into the new common data set through APIs or orchestration integration; and automation and machine learning can ease the skills shortage. He condenses this into three words: simplify, integrate, automate.

talks.title: Cyber Security as the Foundation for the UK’s Digital Transformation
talks.teaser: Explores how UK organisations can secure hybrid working, adopt zero trust and close cyber skills gaps.
talks.summary:
The session is a conversation between Chris Perkins of Microsoft UK and host Andy Trotman. Perkins starts with the pressure the pandemic put on UK organisations, which moved staff to home working almost overnight and had to secure access and identity for dispersed workforces. He also cites a reported 300 percent rise in identity attacks in 2020 and a skills shortage, with 43 percent of organisations finding vacancies hard to fill.

Perkins argues that security enables hybrid working and recommends a zero trust approach: assume breach, verify explicitly and grant least-privilege access. He says this mindset let Microsoft limit the blast radius and recover quickly from the SolarWinds and Nobelium incident. Pete Cooper, from the Government Security Group, joins the discussion and says the shift to remote work put huge pressure on cyber teams, which must keep pace with change while threat actors probe every weakness. Organisations now need to re-examine their assumptions as they reposition their defences for hybrid working.

Cooper's main advice is that cyber risk must be understood at every level of an organisation, with time and clear channels to discuss, escalate and manage it, so leaders share one view of the risk. He closes by recommending that organisations keep routine security hygiene and hold regular internal conversations about security, drawing on the wider community of private sector and research bodies willing to help.
